title: China Presses a Weakness in America’s Tech Policy
gist: US chip strategy has focused for a decade on physical chokepoints (fabs, lithography, minerals), but the instruction set architecture -- the x86/Arm duopoly governing the 'language' chips speak -- has emerged as a barely-considered new chokepoint that policymakers must now address.

themes.theme: Instruction set architecture is a new, overlooked semiconductor chokepoint

insights.claim: For the past decade Washington has worked to secure the physical choke points of the semiconductor industry -- fabrication plants, lithography equipment, advanced packaging and critical minerals -- and the handful of companies that dominate each.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: Frames the established US chip-strategy playbook against which the new ISA chokepoint is being contrasted.
insights.locator: Washington has spent the past decade working

insights.claim: A new chokepoint has emerged in a part of the semiconductor industry that policymakers have barely considered: the instruction set architecture (ISA), the language through which software tells a chip's processor what to do.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: Identifies a specific, under-the-radar policy gap -- ISA control -- that investors in chip design and IP-licensing names should watch for new US export-control or policy action.
insights.locator: Now a new choke point has emerged

insights.claim: America's semiconductor strategy must now confront not only who controls the factories, tools and materials required to make chips, but also who controls the language those chips speak.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: Reframes chip-supply-chain risk beyond manufacturing/equipment to include architecture-level control, widening the set of relevant chokepoints for national-security and investment analysis.
insights.locator: America’s semiconductor strategy now must confront

themes.theme: x86 and Arm's duopoly and differing business models

insights.claim: For more than two decades, two ISAs have dominated mainstream computing: x86, which powers most personal computers and servers, and Arm, which dominates smartphones and is expanding into cars, defense systems and artificial intelligence.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: Confirms the x86/Arm duopoly and Arm's expansion into AI and defense as the backdrop against which any new ISA-related policy risk would play out.
insights.locator: For more than two decades, two ISAs have dominated

insights.claim: x86 and Arm operate through different business models: x86 is used almost exclusively by Intel and AMD, while Arm has historically licensed its technology broadly to other chip designers.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: The licensing-vs-proprietary split matters for how a new ISA policy chokepoint would differentially affect Intel/AMD versus the broader Arm licensee ecosystem.
insights.locator: The two operate through different business models
